Two gates stand between your design and your data. They are different
kinds of thing.

The **IRB** is an ethics review. It governs research involving people.

A **data-use agreement** is a contract. It governs somebody else's
proprietary data.

Both take longer than teams expect. Both have to start in the autumn.
Neither is something you can grant yourself.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Does your project collect data from people?** A survey, an interview,
an experiment. If so, start this in October, not February.

The review itself is often quick. Assembling what it needs is not. And
training has to be finished before anything can be approved.

If you use only existing data about firms, prices, places or securities,
you almost certainly need none of this. Read the first section anyway.
"Existing data about people" is the case that catches teams out.
:::

## Does this apply to us?

The IRB governs **research with human participants.** Two questions
decide it:

1. **Is it research?** A systematic investigation designed to produce
   generalisable knowledge. A capstone intended to inform one firm's
   decision may not be; one written to say something about people in
   general is.
2. **Are there human participants?** Either you interact with living
   people --- surveys, interviews, experiments, focus groups --- or you
   use **identifiable private information** about them.

Teams miss the second half. Scraped social media posts count if
individuals are identifiable. So do purchased consumer records and
administrative microdata.

Cornell's IRB office publishes the
[decision tree](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/sites/default/files/2019-05/IRB%20Decision%20Tree.pdf)
its own staff use, and it has a branch for class projects. A project
whose *sole intent* is to meet a course requirement, with no intention to
use the results for anything else, is not human participant research. A
project whose results leave the course, for a publication, a presentation,
a thesis or a sponsor's decision, is. A capstone is the second kind. The
tree has a second page for existing data, and the question it asks is
whether you can link a row to a living person, directly or through a code,
not what the vendor calls the file.

Foot-traffic and card-spend data of the kind on Dewey arrive aggregated
and de-identified. That is normally what puts them outside the
definition. But **you do not get to make that call yourself.** When in
doubt, ask, and ask early.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**You are not the one who decides you are exempt.** Even exempt research
needs a determination *from the IRB*. "We decided it was exempt" is not
a category.
:::

## How it works at Cornell

The IRB is administered by [**Cornell Research
Services**](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/offices/IRB), East Hill
Office Building.

**Submissions go through RASS-IRB** — [rass.cornell.edu/irb](https://rass.cornell.edu/irb),
with step-by-step guidance at
[guide.rass.cornell.edu](https://guide.rass.cornell.edu).

**Training comes first.** Every person
listed on a protocol must complete
[**CITI Program**](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/training/citi-online-courses-cornell-researchers-coi-irb-rcr-export-control)
human-participants training. That includes **exempt** protocols, a
requirement since October 2022. It lasts five years.

**The IRB issues nothing until every listed person has finished.** One
teammate who skipped the modules holds up the whole team.

The CITI modules are **required of every member of a team whose project
involves human participants**, and session B of
[meeting 4](sessions/04-ethics.qmd) is where each team decides whether
that is you. Register at
[citiprogram.org](https://www.citiprogram.org) under the Cornell
affiliation, take the course Cornell accepts (it is called IRB Training or
IRB Basic), and upload the completion certificate to Canvas before
meeting 6, **Wednesday September 30**. Not there by then costs five
participation points. The modules take two to four hours. If your project
has no human participants you owe nothing now; if the plan changes later,
do the modules that week, before the protocol is drafted. The credential
lasts five years and is worth having for the research most of you will run
inside a firm.

**Three levels of review:**

| Level | Roughly | What it covers |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Exempt** | Most classroom surveys of adults on non-sensitive topics | Still requires an IRB determination |
| **Expedited** | Minimal-risk research not fitting an exempt category | Reviewed by a member, not the full board |
| **Full board** | More than minimal risk, or vulnerable populations | Meets on a schedule — plan around it |

Cornell's own clock, from the IRB office's page on
[the life cycle of a protocol](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/life-cycle-irb-protocol):
an exemption takes **three to four weeks** from start to finish, expedited
review **four to six**, and the full board **four to eight**. The board
meets on the first Friday of every month, so its clock is a calendar, not
a queue. All three assume a complete submission; an incomplete one goes
back and the clock restarts.

Cornell's own guidance for studies enrolling students asks for
submission **at least four weeks before** enrolment begins, and warns
that anything needing an ancillary review takes longer.

## What this means for your timeline

| When | What |
|:--|:--|
| **By September 30 (meeting 6)** | Teams with human participants complete CITI training and upload the certificate to Canvas. Required and graded for them |
| **Meeting 9–10 (late Oct)** | You know whether your design needs human participants |
| **Late Oct / early Nov** | Draft the protocol: instrument, consent language, recruitment, data handling |
| **November** | Submit through RASS-IRB |
| **Spring (AEM 6992)** | Collect |

The point of doing it in the fall is that **AEM 6992 is where you
execute.** A protocol still in review in February costs you a third of
the semester you were going to run the study in.

## What a protocol actually asks for

Less than students fear, but all of it in writing:

- **What you will do**, step by step, from recruitment to analysis
- **Who your participants are**, how many, and how you find them
- **The instrument itself** — the actual survey, the actual script
- **Consent language** — what you tell people before they agree
- **Risks and benefits**, stated honestly. For most survey work the risk
  is boredom and a small privacy exposure; say so rather than claiming
  zero
- **Data handling** — where it lives, who sees it, whether it is
  identifiable, when it is destroyed
- **A faculty member**, since students generally cannot serve as
  principal investigator on their own. That is me. I am the faculty
  advisor on your protocol, so the draft goes past me before it goes to
  the IRB

Writing the instrument early is not bureaucracy tax. It forces you to
decide what you are actually measuring, which is
[meeting 4](sessions/04-ethics.qmd).

## Data-use agreements

The second gate, and a different animal. A DUA is a **contract**, not an
ethics review, and it is signed by **the university** rather than by
you — which is why you cannot simply accept a firm's terms on your
team's behalf, however reasonable they look. If a firm gives you proprietary data,
expect legal review on both sides, expect it to take months, and expect
restrictions on what you may publish.

At Cornell the
[Office of Sponsored Programs](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/exchange-commercially-unavailablerestricted-data)
is the party that enters into agreements for the use of data. Write to
osp_dua@cornell.edu, and ask in October whether it will sign for a
capstone team rather than assuming it will. The agreement binds the
university, and it binds you through the university.

Read the licence on data you already have, too. Most of what the library
pays for, WRDS and Compustat included, is licensed for **academic,
non-commercial use**. A project a firm would pay for cannot be built on a
file whose licence forbids commercial use.

Two consequences worth planning around: **you may not be able to show
your results**, and the agreement may not be signed in time. If your
project depends on a DUA, it needs a plan B by
[meeting 5](sessions/05-tools-and-ai.qmd).

## Where the file lives

Cornell classifies data as
[low, moderate or high risk](https://it.cornell.edu/regulated-data).
Anything under FERPA sits at moderate risk. Identifiers paired with a
name, health records and financial account data sit at high risk.
Proprietary and licensed data are covered by the same rule.

**Nothing at moderate risk or above goes into a publicly available AI
tool.** That is Cornell's rule, in
[its own words](https://innovationhub.ai.cornell.edu/tools-resources/),
and anything you put into a public tool is treated as public. The approved
tools are listed on that page. If the file you hold is not one you may
upload, the assistant sees the column names and five invented rows, and
the code it writes runs on your laptop.

Removing the names is not de-identification. ZIP code, birth date and sex
together
[identify most Americans uniquely](https://dataprivacylab.org/projects/identifiability/paper1.pdf).
Coarsen what you do not need at full resolution, and collect only what the
question needs.

## Where to ask

- The IRB office answers questions before submission, and would much
  rather hear from you early than fix a protocol later.
- Ask me first if you are unsure whether any of this applies. Usually it
  does not take long to find out, and the answer changes what you can
  design.
